questions.question: Which ancient site in India is the chosen location for the construction of the 'National Maritime Heritage Complex', a significant project dedicated to displaying India's rich maritime history?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lothal, Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Lothal**, located in Gujarat, is one of the most prominent cities of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization and an important site for its maritime connections.
 
• The **National Maritime Heritage Complex (NMHC)** is being developed at Lothal to showcase India’s rich maritime history and its connection to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization.
 
• This complex will include world-class museums, heritage parks, and an aquarium dedicated to maritime activities, making it a global tourist attraction.
 
• As per the latest updates, the NMHC is part of the **‘Sagar Mala Project’**, which aims to modernize India’s ports and develop coastal areas.
 
• The site of Lothal was specifically chosen for its historical significance as it was a major trade center and port during 2400 BCE to 1900 BCE.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dwarka, Gujarat:**

 
 
• Dwarka, located on the western coast of Gujarat, is a significant religious site and one of the **Char Dham pilgrimage destinations** in Hinduism.
 
• It is associated with the legend of Lord Krishna, who is believed to have established his kingdom here.
 
• The underwater explorations near Dwarka have revealed structures that are believed to be parts of an ancient submerged city, often referred to as the ‘Lost City of Dwarka.’
 
• Despite its maritime significance, it was not chosen for the NMHC project.
 
 
 
• **Poompuhar, Tamil Nadu:**
 
 
• Poompuhar, also known as Kaveripattinam, was an ancient port city of the Chola dynasty, located in Tamil Nadu.
 
• It served as a major center for maritime trade and cultural exchange with Southeast Asia during the Sangam period.
 
• The remains of the city have been submerged, and underwater archaeological studies are ongoing to explore its history.
 
• While Poompuhar holds historical importance, it was not selected for the NMHC project.
 
 
 
• **Chandraketugarh, West Bengal:**
 
 
• Chandraketugarh is an archaeological site located near Kolkata in West Bengal, known for its rich historical artifacts from the Mauryan and Gupta periods.
 
• This site has provided important evidence of ancient trade and cultural practices in eastern India.
 
• It is more significant for its terrestrial archaeological findings rather than maritime history, which is why it was not considered for the NMHC.
 
 
 
• **National Maritime Heritage Complex (NMHC):**
 
 
• The NMHC is designed to be a state-of-the-art facility to preserve and display India’s maritime heritage, which dates back to the Harappan civilization.
 
• It aims to promote awareness of India’s historical and cultural connection with the maritime world and is being developed as a key component of India’s maritime diplomacy and coastal tourism.
 
• The complex will feature numerous exhibits, including ancient navigation techniques, shipbuilding technologies, and artifacts from maritime trade routes.

questions.question: The Hindi novel Godaan, which depicts rural struggles, social realities, and the plight of farmers in pre-independence India, was authored by _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Premchand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Godaan** is considered one of the most celebrated novels in Hindi literature, authored by Premchand in 1936.
 
• The novel portrays the hardships and struggles of rural farmers in pre-independence India, highlighting issues such as poverty, social exploitation, and the caste system.
 
• Premchand, known as the “Upanyas Samrat” (Emperor of Novels), is regarded as one of the most influential writers in Hindi and Urdu literature.
 
• Godaan is recognized for its realistic narrative and depiction of rural life, focusing on the protagonist Hori Mahato and his pursuit of dignity amidst societal challenges.
 
• Premchand’s works often addressed social issues such as injustice, inequality, and the plight of marginalized communities, showcasing his reformist ideology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahadevi Verma:**

 
 
• Mahadevi Verma was a prominent Hindi poet and writer, known for her contributions to the Chhayavad movement in Hindi literature.
 
• She was awarded the Padma Bhushan and Padma Vibhushan for her literary achievements.
 
• Her notable works include “Madhur Madhur Mere Deepak” and “Yama,” which reflect themes of love, spirituality, and human emotions.
 
 
 
• **Ramdhari Singh 'Dinkar':**
 
 
• Ramdhari Singh 'Dinkar' was a renowned Hindi poet, often referred to as “Rashtrakavi” or National Poet.
 
• He is best known for his patriotic and nationalist poetry, including works like “Rashmirathi” and “Parashuram Ki Pratiksha.”
 
• His writings reflect themes of heroism, valor, and social reform.
 
 
 
• **Nagarjun:**
 
 
• Nagarjun was a celebrated Hindi and Maithili poet known for his progressive and socially conscious literary works.
 
• His poetry often addressed themes of social injustice, politics, and the struggles of the common man.
 
• Some of his notable works include “Harijan Gatha” and “Ratinath Ki Chachi.”
 
 
 
• **Main Theme:**
 
 
• The question revolves around the Hindi novel “Godaan,” which is a masterpiece depicting rural struggles, social realities, and the plight of farmers in pre-independence India.
 
• The novel is a significant reflection of Indian society during colonial times, addressing poverty, exploitation, and the resilience of marginalized communities.

questions.question: The title 'Iron Man of India' is famously attributed to which personality, known for their pivotal role in unifying princely states and strengthening India's national integration after independence?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vallabhbhai Patel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, popularly known as the **Iron Man of India**, played a significant role in the integration of the princely states into independent India post-1947.
 
• He was the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India and is credited with unifying over 560 princely states to form the modern Indian Union.
 
• Through his diplomatic skills and firm approach, Patel successfully convinced rulers of princely states to accede to India, often overcoming significant resistance.
 
• Patel was instrumental in the peaceful accession of major princely states such as Hyderabad, Junagadh, and Jammu & Kashmir into India.
 
• His efforts in nation-building earned him the title "Iron Man," reflecting his steadfastness and determination in preserving India's territorial integrity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru**

 
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister of India and a key figure in the Indian independence movement.
 
• He laid the foundation for India's parliamentary democracy and was a strong proponent of industrialization and scientific development.
 
• Under his leadership, India adopted a policy of non-alignment during the Cold War.
 
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**
 
 
• Mahatma Gandhi, known as the Father of the Nation, was the leader of India's non-violent independence movement against British rule.
 
• He introduced the principles of satyagraha (truth and non-violence) and led movements like the Salt March and Quit India Movement.
 
• While he was not directly involved in the unification of princely states, his philosophy greatly influenced Indian leaders like Patel and Nehru.
 
 
 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai**
 
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai was one of the prominent leaders of the Indian Nationalist Movement and is often referred to as the "Punjab Kesari" (Lion of Punjab).
 
• He played an important role in the freedom struggle and was part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio, which advocated Swadeshi and boycotting foreign goods.
 
• Though he contributed significantly to the independence movement, he was not involved in post-independence state unification efforts.
 
 
 
• **Integration of Princely States**
 
 
• At the time of India's independence in 1947, there were over 560 princely states that had the option to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent.
 
• Through the efforts of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon, most states acceded to India, ensuring the country's territorial integrity.
 
• This process was crucial in laying the foundation for a unified and stable Indian nation-state.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution specifies the provisions regarding the disqualification of Members of Parliament on the grounds of holding an 'Office of Profit'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 102**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 102** of the Indian Constitution specifies the grounds for disqualification of Members of Parliament (MPs) in India.
 
• It states that an MP can be disqualified if they hold an **'Office of Profit'**, are of unsound mind, are undischarged insolvents, or are not a citizen of India.
 
• The term **'Office of Profit'** refers to a position that brings financial benefits from the government and may lead to a conflict of interest for a legislator.
 
• The disqualification is determined by the **President of India** in consultation with the Election Commission as per Article 103.
 
• This provision ensures the **separation of powers** and prevents MPs from misusing their position for personal gain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 79**

 
 
• This article deals with the **Constitution of Parliament** in India.
 
• It states that the Parliament consists of the **President**, the **Council of States (Rajya Sabha)**, and the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)**.
 
• It forms the legislative framework for the Indian parliamentary system.
 
 
 
• **Article 80**
 
 
• Article 80 specifies the composition of the **Rajya Sabha (Council of States)**.
 
• It mentions the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha, which is **250 members**.
 
• Out of these, **12 members are nominated by the President** for their expertise in various fields such as literature, science, art, and social service.
 
• The rest are elected by the legislative assemblies of the states and union territories.
 
 
 
• **Article 324**
 
 
• This article vests the **superintendence, direction, and control** of elections in the hands of the **Election Commission of India (ECI)**.
 
• The ECI is responsible for conducting free and fair elections to the Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice-President.
 
• It ensures the democratic functioning of the electoral process in India.

questions.question: The Constitution of India was formally approved by the Constituent Assembly on ______, prior to its complete enforcement on 26 January 1950.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**26th November 1949**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Constitution of India was formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly on **26th November 1949**.
 
• On this day, the Constituent Assembly completed its work on drafting the Constitution, which had been in progress for nearly three years.
 
• The Constitution came into full effect on **26th January 1950**, a date chosen to honor the declaration of Purna Swaraj (complete independence) in 1930.
 
• 26th November is celebrated annually as **Constitution Day**, also known as "Samvidhan Divas," in India since 2015.
 
• The Indian Constitution is the **longest written Constitution in the world**, containing 395 Articles and 8 Schedules at the time of its adoption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **25th November 1949:**

 
 
• This date marks the penultimate session of the Constituent Assembly.
 
• The Assembly discussed the final draft of the Constitution but did not formally adopt it on this date.
 
 
 
• **26th October 1949:**
 
 
• No significant event related to the Constitution of India occurred on this date.
 
• It is not associated with the drafting, adoption, or implementation of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **22nd January 1950:**
 
 
• This date falls during the transitional period between the adoption of the Constitution on 26th November 1949 and its enforcement on 26th January 1950.
 
• It holds no particular relevance to the formal adoption or enforcement of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Significance of 26th January 1950:**
 
 
• The Constitution of India came into force on this date, marking the beginning of the Republic of India.
 
• The date was chosen to commemorate the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in 1930, which declared Purna Swaraj.

questions.question: During Alauddin Khalji's reign, which general led the significant invasions of South India (Deccan)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Malik Kafur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Malik Kafur was a prominent general during the reign of Alauddin Khalji, the Sultan of Delhi, and played a key role in expanding the Sultanate's territories.
 
• He led successful military expeditions to South India (Deccan) between 1309 and 1311, conquering kingdoms such as the Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiyas of Warangal, the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra, and the Pandyas of Madurai.
 
• Malik Kafur's invasions brought immense wealth to the Delhi Sultanate, including precious jewels, gold, and other riches from South Indian temples and royal treasuries.
 
• He was a trusted lieutenant of Alauddin Khalji, known for his military acumen and loyalty, which earned him the title "Hazardinari" as he was initially purchased as a slave for 1,000 dinars.
 
• Malik Kafur's campaigns marked the northern expansion into the Deccan and contributed significantly to Alauddin Khalji's ambition of consolidating his empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nusrat Khan**

 
 
• Nusrat Khan was another prominent general under Alauddin Khalji and played a key role in the early military campaigns of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• He was instrumental in the conquest of Gujarat in 1299 and the suppression of rebellions in northern India during Alauddin's reign.
 
• However, Nusrat Khan was not associated with the Deccan campaigns led by Malik Kafur.
 
 
 
• **Ain-ul-Mulk Multani**
 
 
• Ain-ul-Mulk Multani was a noble and governor under Alauddin Khalji who was entrusted with administrative duties and military expeditions.
 
• He was primarily involved in campaigns against Rajput rulers and rebellions in northern India, such as the suppression of the revolt in Gujarat.
 
• He did not lead the invasions of South India.
 
 
 
• **Ghazi Malik**
 
 
• Ghazi Malik, later known as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, was a governor under Alauddin Khalji and eventually the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty.
 
• He was known for his military campaigns in the north-western regions of India but had no direct involvement in the Deccan invasions.
 
 
 
• **Overview of Alauddin Khalji's Deccan Campaigns**
 
 
• The Deccan campaigns were a significant milestone in the history of the Delhi Sultanate, marking the first major incursions into South India.
 
• Alauddin Khalji's ambition to control the wealth and resources of the Deccan led to these expeditions under the leadership of Malik Kafur.
 
• The campaigns demonstrated the military superiority of the Sultanate while showcasing the strategic importance of South India in medieval Indian history.

questions.question: Which journalist is credited with authoring 'Everybody Loves a Good Drought', a book that documents rural poverty and agrarian distress in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**P. Sainath**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **P. Sainath** is a distinguished Indian journalist and author who is renowned for his work on rural poverty and agrarian issues in India.
 
• His book ‘Everybody Loves a Good Drought’__ (1996) documents the struggles of rural India, focusing on poverty, social issues, and the failures of government policies in addressing these problems.
 
• The book is based on extensive fieldwork in some of the poorest and drought-prone regions of India, providing vivid and detailed accounts of the lives of rural communities.
 
• ‘Everybody Loves a Good Drought’ is considered a seminal work in Indian journalism and has won several accolades, including the prestigious **Ramon Magsaysay Award for Journalism, Literature, and Creative Communication Arts** in 2007.
 
• P. Sainath’s work has been influential in raising awareness about rural distress and the need for inclusive policies to address agrarian crises in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Barkha Dutt:**

 
 
• Barkha Dutt is a prominent Indian television journalist, columnist, and author.
 
• She gained recognition for her coverage of the Kargil War in 1999 and has been a recipient of several journalism awards, including the **Padma Shri**.
 
• She is known for her work on gender issues, politics, and social justice but is not associated with rural and agrarian issues at the level of P. Sainath.
 
 
 
• **Ravish Kumar:**
 
 
• Ravish Kumar is a well-known journalist and television anchor in India, primarily associated with **NDTV India**.
 
• He is known for his critical reporting on political, social, and economic issues and has been a vocal advocate for press freedom.
 
• Ravish Kumar won the prestigious **Ramon Magsaysay Award** in 2019 for his fearless journalism but does not focus exclusively on rural poverty and agrarian issues.
 
 
 
• **Rajdeep Sardesai:**
 
 
• Rajdeep Sardesai is a senior Indian journalist, author, and news anchor, known for his work in television journalism.
 
• He has written books on Indian politics, including ‘2014: The Election that Changed India’__, which focuses on electoral politics rather than rural or agrarian issues.
 
• While a respected journalist, his work does not specifically address the themes of rural poverty and agrarian distress covered in P. Sainath’s book.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme:**
 __
 
• The book ‘Everybody Loves a Good Drought’__ sheds light on the systemic neglect of rural India by policymakers and highlights the resilience of rural communities in facing poverty and natural calamities.
 
• It remains a critical resource for understanding the socio-economic challenges of rural India and the need for sustainable and inclusive development.

questions.question: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj signed the 'Treaty of Purandar' (1665), ceding forts to the Mughals, after being defeated by Mughal general ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Raja Jai Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Raja Jai Singh I was a prominent military leader and diplomat under Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb.
 
• He led the Mughal forces against Shivaji during the campaign that culminated in the signing of the Treaty of Purandar in 1665.
 
• The Treaty of Purandar required Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj to surrender 23 forts and territory worth an annual revenue of ₹4 lakh to the Mughals.
 
• Under the treaty, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj agreed to become a vassal of the Mughal Empire and assist the Mughals in their Deccan campaigns.
 
• Raja Jai Singh's diplomatic skills were instrumental in negotiating this treaty and securing the submission of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, who later escaped Mughal captivity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Jaswant Singh**

 
 
• Jaswant Singh was another Rajput general under the Mughal Empire, but he was not involved in the Treaty of Purandar.
 
• He played a significant role in various Mughal military campaigns but did not lead forces against Shivaji.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: Bahadur Khan**
 
 
• Bahadur Khan was a Mughal commander known for his involvement in other military campaigns, especially in the Deccan region.
 
• He did not negotiate or lead the forces against Shivaji during the Treaty of Purandar.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Ibrahim Khan**
 
 
• Ibrahim Khan was a Mughal officer but did not have any role in the Treaty of Purandar or in the campaigns against Shivaji.
 
 
 
• **Theme of the Question: Treaty of Purandar (1665)**
 
 
• The Treaty of Purandar was signed in 1665 between Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and the Mughal Empire, represented by Raja Jai Singh.
 
• This treaty marked a temporary setback for Shivaji, who ceded territory and agreed to serve as a Mughal vassal.
 
• Despite his submission, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj later escaped from Mughal captivity and resumed his resistance against Mughal rule.
 
• The treaty is considered a turning point in Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj's struggle against the Mughals and demonstrates his strategic acumen in dealing with powerful adversaries.

questions.question: The 'Iqta' system, a method of assigning land revenue to nobles instead of wages, was first implemented by which Sultan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iltutmish**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Iltutmish**, the Sultan of Delhi (1211–1236), was the first ruler to institutionalize the **'Iqta' system** in India.
 
• The 'Iqta' system involved granting land revenue assignments to nobles or officers in lieu of salaries, ensuring administrative efficiency and loyalty.
 
• The system was borrowed from Persian traditions and adapted to suit the Indian context under Iltutmish’s reign.
 
• The 'Iqta' holders (known as 'Iqtadars') were responsible for maintaining law and order, collecting revenue, and providing military services to the Sultan.
 
• This system helped in consolidating and centralizing the Sultanate’s administration and ensured the financial stability of the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Razia Sultan:**

 
 
• Razia Sultan was the first and only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, ruling from 1236 to 1240.
 
• She was known for her administrative reforms and efforts to reduce the influence of Turkish nobles.
 
• Razia Sultan did not implement the Iqta system but focused on strengthening her authority amidst challenges from nobles and elites.
 
 
 
• **Nasiruddin Mahmud:**
 
 
• Nasiruddin Mahmud was the Sultan of Delhi from 1246 to 1266, known for his simplicity and religious devotion.
 
• He relied heavily on his Prime Minister Balban for administration and military matters.
 
• The Iqta system was already established before his reign, and Nasiruddin did not contribute significantly to its development.
 
 
 
• **Jalaluddin Khalji:**
 
 
• Jalaluddin Khalji was the founder of the Khalji dynasty and ruled from 1290 to 1296.
 
• While he implemented several administrative reforms, his tenure focused more on consolidating power and dealing with Mongol invasions.
 
• He did not introduce or modify the Iqta system significantly during his reign.
 
 
 
• **The Iqta System:**
 
 
• The Iqta system was an important administrative mechanism in medieval India, particularly during the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• It ensured the effective governance of distant territories by delegating responsibilities to nobles and officers.
 
• The system facilitated military support to the Sultan and streamlined revenue collection, serving as the backbone of the Sultanate’s administration.

questions.question: An increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) by the RBI immediately results in banks having ______ money to lend.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**less**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** is the proportion of total deposits that banks are required to maintain with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as reserves.
 
• An increase in CRR means that banks must keep a higher percentage of their deposits with the RBI, reducing the amount of money available for lending.
 
• This measure is often used by the RBI to control inflation and regulate liquidity in the economy by restricting the flow of credit.
 
• Higher CRR reduces the funds that banks can use for loans and investments, as a larger portion of their deposits is locked with the RBI.
 
• **CRR changes impact the banking system immediately** as banks are required to comply on the very day the change is implemented.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: More**

 
 
• An increase in CRR would not result in banks having more money to lend. Instead, it reduces their lending capacity as they are required to hold more funds with the RBI.
 
• Having "more money to lend" would occur if CRR is reduced, allowing banks to retain a larger portion of their deposits for lending purposes.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Equal**
 
 
• If CRR is increased, banks do not retain an equal amount of money as before for lending. Instead, their lending capacity decreases because a larger portion of their deposits is now held by the RBI.
 
• Equal money to lend would occur only if there is no change in the CRR.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Unlimited**
 
 
• Banks never have unlimited money to lend, as their lending capacity is constrained by regulatory requirements such as CRR and the availability of deposits.
 
• Unlimited lending is also restricted by other banking norms like the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and capital adequacy requirements.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)**
 
 
• CRR is a critical monetary policy tool used by the RBI to manage liquidity in the economy.
 
• By adjusting CRR, the RBI can influence credit creation, inflation control, and overall economic stability.
 
• CRR is expressed as a percentage of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) of banks.
 
• It ensures that banks maintain a minimum reserve to safeguard against financial risks.

questions.question: Disinvestment (selling shares of PSUs) is classified under the part of the Budget known as _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Capital Receipts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Capital Receipts** include funds raised by the government through borrowing, disinvestment, or recovery of loans. These are non-recurring in nature.
 
• Disinvestment refers to the process of selling stakes in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and is categorized under capital receipts because it involves the transfer of capital assets.
 
• The proceeds from disinvestment are utilized by the government for reducing the fiscal deficit, financing developmental projects, or other expenditure needs.
 
• Examples of capital receipts include loans raised by the government, external borrowings, proceeds from disinvestment, and small savings collections.
 
• Capital receipts do not result in the creation of liabilities or reduction of assets, except when disinvestment or loans are involved.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Current Account Receipts**

 
 
• These include the regular flow of funds received by the government such as tax revenue, non-tax revenue, and other receipts.
 
• Examples include income tax, customs duty, excise duty, and dividends from PSUs.
 
• Current account receipts are recurring in nature and contribute to the government’s day-to-day expenses.
 
• Unlike capital receipts, current account receipts do not involve the sale of assets or borrowing.
 
 
 
• **Operating Expenditure**
 
 
• It refers to the day-to-day expenses incurred by the government for running various departments and institutions.
 
• Examples include salaries of government employees, pensions, subsidies, and maintenance costs.
 
• Operating expenditure is a part of revenue expenditure and is financed through current account receipts.
 
• This type of expenditure does not lead to the creation of assets or reduction of liabilities.
 
 
 
• **Investment Outlays**
 
 
• Investment outlays refer to the funds allocated by the government for capital formation and development projects.
 
• These include expenditure on infrastructure such as roads, railways, power plants, and irrigation facilities.
 
• Unlike disinvestment, investment outlays are considered as capital expenditure aimed at asset creation.
 
• They contribute to long-term economic growth and development.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Disinvestment**
 
 
• Disinvestment involves the sale of government-owned shares in public sector enterprises to private entities or individuals.

questions.question: Money that has no intrinsic value but is declared as money by government order is known as ____.

__
 
• **Fiat money** is a type of currency that has no intrinsic value; its value is derived solely from the trust and recognition of the government or issuing authority.
 
• It is not backed by a physical commodity like gold or silver, unlike representative or metallic money.
 
• The government declares fiat money as legal tender, meaning it must be accepted as a medium of exchange for goods and services.
 
• The value of fiat money is maintained by the stability and economic policies of the issuing government.
 
• Examples of fiat money include most modern currencies like the Indian Rupee (INR), US Dollar (USD), and Euro (EUR).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Metallic Money**

 
 
• Metallic money refers to currency made from metals such as gold, silver, or copper.
 
• It has intrinsic value because the metal itself has value independent of its use as money.
 
• Historically, metallic money was used widely before the advent of paper currency and fiat money.
 
• The weight and purity of the metal determined its value.
 
 
 
• **Representative Money**
 
 
• Representative money is a type of currency that represents a claim on a commodity, such as gold or silver, which can be redeemed upon demand.
 
• It has no intrinsic value but is backed by a physical asset held in reserve by a central authority or bank.
 
• Examples include gold certificates or silver certificates issued in the past.
 
 
 
• **Token Money**
 
 
• Token money refers to coins or notes with a face value greater than their intrinsic or material value.
 
• For example, a coin made of inexpensive metal may have a purchasing power higher than the value of the metal it is made from.
 
• It is used as a medium of exchange and is accepted because of government backing.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme of the Question: Money**
 
 
• Money is a medium of exchange that facilitates trade and economic transactions.
 
• It can exist in various forms, including metallic money, fiat money, representative money, and token money.
 
• Modern economies rely heavily on fiat money as it is convenient and cost-effective to produce and manage.

questions.question: The Chalukya Vesara architectural style, a unique hybrid of Dravidian and Nagara traditions found in medieval Karnataka, is best exemplified by which of the following temple complexes?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Pattadakal Temples, located in Karnataka, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and showcase the unique **Chalukya Vesara style of architecture.**
 
• This architectural style is a hybrid of **Dravidian (South Indian temple architecture) and Nagara (North Indian temple architecture) traditions**, reflecting the cultural fusion of medieval India.
 
• The temples at Pattadakal were constructed during the reign of the Chalukya dynasty, particularly in the 7th and 8th centuries CE.
 
• The complex consists of several temples, such as the Virupaksha Temple and Mallikarjuna Temple, which are **excellent examples of Vesara architecture, blending intricate carvings and unique structural designs.**
 
• The Virupaksha Temple was built by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate her husband King Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas, and it is considered a masterpiece of this architectural style.
 
• The site is recognized for its cultural significance and artistic achievements, making it an important heritage landmark in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Located in Gujarat, the Sun Temple at Modhera was built during the reign of the Solanki dynasty in the 11th century CE.
 
• It is dedicated to Surya, the Sun God, and is an example of the **Nagara style of architecture**, characterized by its curvilinear shikhara (tower) and intricate carvings.
 
• The temple complex includes a sanctum, a hall, and a stepped tank called the Surya Kund, used for ritualistic purposes.
 
• While it is an architectural marvel, it does not represent the Vesara style, as it strictly follows the Nagara tradition.

• The Brihadeeswarar Temple, also known as the Big Temple, is located in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, and is dedicated to Lord Shiva.
 
• It was built by Raja Raja Chola I in the 11th century CE and is a prime example of **Dravidian architecture**, characterized by its massive vimana (tower) and elaborate sculptures.
 
• The temple is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Great Living Chola Temples" and showcases the grandeur of Chola architecture.
 
• While it is architecturally significant, it does not represent the hybrid Vesara style.
 
 
 
• **Dilwara Temples**
 
 
• Located in Mount Abu, Rajasthan, the Dilwara Temples are a group of Jain temples constructed between the 11th and 13th centuries CE.
 
• They are renowned for their **marble craftsmanship and intricate carvings**, particularly in the ceilings and pillars.
 
• The architectural style of these temples is distinct from Vesara; they reflect Jain temple architectural traditions.
 
• The temples are dedicated to various Jain Tirthankaras and hold significant religious importance for the Jain community.
 
 
 
• **Chalukya Vesara Style of Architecture**
 
 
• The Vesara style emerged during the reign of the Chalukyas and later developed further under the Rashtrakutas and Hoysalas.
 
• This style is a fusion of the Dravidian and Nagara traditions, combining elements like stepped vimanas, intricate carvings, and distinct temple layouts.
 
• The Pattadakal Temples are the most prominent examples of this style, showcasing the artistic and cultural innovations of the Chalukya dynasty.

• In a regular game of table tennis, a player must score **11 points to win**, provided they maintain a lead of at least two points over their opponent.

• The 11-point format is used in both individual matches and professional tournaments worldwide.

questions.question: In international trade, a 'tariff' is defined as ______.

options.text: A restriction on the quantity of goods traded
A direct tax on corporate profits
A government payment to domestic industries

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A tax on imported goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A tariff is a tax or duty imposed by a government on goods that are imported from other countries.
 
• The primary purpose of a tariff is to restrict imports by increasing the price of goods and services purchased from overseas, making them less attractive to domestic consumers.
 
• Tariffs are often used as a tool to protect domestic industries from foreign competition and to boost local manufacturing.
 
• There are two main types of tariffs: **specific tariffs** (a fixed fee per unit of imported goods) and **ad valorem tariffs** (a percentage of the value of the goods).
 
• Tariffs can have both positive and negative effects, such as promoting domestic industries while potentially leading to higher prices for consumers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **A restriction on the quantity of goods traded:**

 
 
• This refers to a **quota**, not a tariff. A quota sets a physical limit on the quantity of specific goods that can be imported or exported during a given time frame.
 
• Quotas are often used to protect domestic industries by limiting foreign competition.
 
• Unlike tariffs, quotas do not generate revenue for the government but directly restrict the volume of trade.
 
 
 
• **A direct tax on corporate profits:**
 
 
• This describes **corporate tax**, which is a tax imposed on the profits earned by businesses and corporations.
 
• Corporate taxes are unrelated to tariffs or international trade. They are a domestic fiscal policy tool used to generate revenue for the government.
 
• Corporate tax rates vary significantly between countries and are often a subject of economic policy discussions.
 
 
 
• **A government payment to domestic industries:**
 
 
• This refers to a **subsidy**, not a tariff. Subsidies are financial aids provided by the government to support domestic industries and make their goods more competitive in the global market.
 
• Subsidies aim to reduce production costs, improve export potential, and protect jobs in specific sectors.
 
• While tariffs increase the price of imports, subsidies lower the cost of domestic production, achieving a similar goal of protecting local industries.

• Article 75(5) of the Indian Constitution states that a Minister who is not a member of Parliament at the time of appointment must get elected to either House of Parliament within **6 months** to continue holding office.

• If the Minister fails to get elected within six months, he/she must vacate the position immediately as per constitutional requirements.
 
• Ministers appointed without being members of Parliament are typically chosen for their expertise or political significance but must gain electoral approval within the stipulated time frame.
 
• This rule applies uniformly to both the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States).

• Such a duration would compromise the principle of timely democratic accountability for Ministers appointed without being elected.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Till the end of the current Lok Sabha term**

• The appointment of Ministers who are not members of Parliament is allowed under the Indian Constitution but comes with the condition of democratic validation.

• It prevents prolonged tenure of unelected individuals in ministerial roles, ensuring that governance remains democratic and accountable.

questions.question: Dramatic facial expressions, known as "Navarasas," which highlight nine emotions for storytelling and are often performed with elaborate costumes and gestures, are a hallmark of which classical dance form?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kathakali** is a traditional classical dance form that originated in the state of **Kerala, India**.
 
• It is known for its **dramatic facial expressions** (Navarasas), elaborate costumes, intricate gestures, and well-defined body movements synchronized with music and vocal performances.
 
• The "Navarasas" (Nine Emotions) include Shringara (love), Hasya (laughter), Karuna (compassion), Raudra (anger), Veera (heroism), Bhayanaka (fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder), and Shanta (peace).
 
• The dance form is a blend of **theatre, dance, and music**, performed to narrate stories from ancient Hindu epics like the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
 
• Performers in Kathakali use heavy makeup, masks, and colorful costumes to enhance their expressions and storytelling abilities, making it a visually rich art form.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Kuchipudi is a classical dance form from **Andhra Pradesh**, India.
 
• It combines graceful movements and rhythmic patterns with expressions and storylines based on Hindu religious themes.
 
• Unlike Kathakali, Kuchipudi often includes dialogue delivery along with dance and songs.
 
• Kuchipudi dancers perform barefoot, wearing traditional attire, and use intricate footwork and subtle facial expressions to narrate stories.
 
 
 
• **Odissi**
 
 
• Odissi is one of the oldest classical dance forms of India, originating from the state of **Odisha**.
 
• It is characterized by **fluid body movements**, intricate gestures, and sculpturesque poses inspired by the temple art of Odisha.
 
• The dance form is traditionally associated with the worship of Lord Jagannath and other Hindu deities.
 
• Odissi performances emphasize the "Tribhangi" (three bends) posture, which is a hallmark of this dance style.
 
 
 
• **Manipuri**
 
 
• Manipuri is a classical dance form originating from **Manipur**, a northeastern state of India.
 
• It is deeply rooted in the **Vaishnavite traditions** and is primarily dedicated to the depiction of the divine love of Radha and Krishna.
 
• The dance form is known for its **graceful and delicate movements**, along with the use of traditional Manipuri costumes.
 
• Unlike Kathakali, Manipuri focuses more on devotion and spirituality, with less emphasis on dramatic expressions.

• The scheme aims to provide **LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) connections** to Below Poverty Line (BPL) households in order to reduce the usage of traditional cooking methods like wood, coal, or cow dung cakes.

• They are not included in the PMUY scheme as they require consistent electricity supply, which might not be available in rural and underprivileged households.
 
• Induction cooktops are an alternative cooking method but are not a focus of government schemes like PMUY.

• Biogas is a renewable energy source produced through the anaerobic digestion of organic waste, such as agricultural residue, cattle dung, and kitchen waste.
 
• While biogas connections are promoted in India under specific renewable energy initiatives, they are not part of the PMUY scheme.
 
• Biogas plants are generally installed for larger-scale rural or community-based cooking and energy needs.

questions.question: Ocean tides on Earth, leading to regular rises and falls in sea levels worldwide, are primarily caused by ______.

options.text: Gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ocean tides are primarily caused by the **gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun** on Earth's water bodies.
 
• The Moon has a stronger effect on Earth's tides than the Sun, as it is much closer to Earth, despite the Sun's greater mass.
 
• The gravitational pull causes water to bulge out on the side of Earth facing the Moon, creating a high tide. A corresponding bulge occurs on the opposite side due to centrifugal forces.
 
• The Sun also contributes to tides, and when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align (during full or new moons), the gravitational forces combine to create **spring tides**, which are higher than usual.
 
• Conversely, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles relative to the Earth, **neap tides** occur, which are lower than usual.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prevailing ocean currents**

 
 
• Ocean currents are continuous, directed movements of seawater generated by forces such as wind, Earth's rotation, and differences in water density.
 
• While currents influence the distribution of heat and nutrients in the ocean, they do not cause the regular rise and fall of sea levels associated with tides.
 
• Examples of major currents include the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio Current, and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
 
 
 
• **Changes in atmospheric pressure**
 
 
• Atmospheric pressure variations can cause localized changes in sea level, known as **storm surges** or **barometric tides**.
 
• These effects are short-term and are usually associated with weather events like cyclones or storms, rather than the periodic tidal patterns caused by gravitational forces.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic activity and seafloor spreading**
 
 
• Volcanic activity and seafloor spreading occur due to tectonic processes and can lead to phenomena such as tsunamis or changes in seafloor topography.
 
• These are geological events and do not contribute to the regular, predictable rise and fall of ocean tides.

questions.question: Which of the following officeholders serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Planning Commission?

• The Planning Commission was established in **1950** by the Government of India to promote economic development and formulate five-year plans.
 
• The **Prime Minister** of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Planning Commission, holding the highest authority in decision-making for the Commission.
 
• The role of the Chairman includes providing strategic direction, approving policy frameworks, and ensuring coordination between ministries and states for achieving developmental goals.
 
• Under the Planning Commission, the Prime Minister played a crucial role in shaping India's economic policies, especially in areas like agriculture, industry, and infrastructure development.
 
• The Planning Commission was replaced by the **NITI Aayog** in 2015, and the Prime Minister continues to serve as its Chairperson.

• Both the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog are chaired by the Prime Minister of India.

questions.question: Due to its massive size and despite its lower density compared to terrestrial planets, ______ has the strongest surface gravity in the Solar System.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jupiter**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Jupiter** is the largest planet in the Solar System, with a diameter of approximately 139,820 km, making it more than 11 times the size of Earth.
 
• Despite being a gas giant primarily composed of hydrogen and helium, Jupiter exhibits the **strongest surface gravity** in the Solar System due to its massive size and high mass.
 
• The surface gravity of Jupiter is approximately **24.79 m/s²**, which is more than twice that of Earth (9.8 m/s²).
 
• Its immense gravitational influence not only impacts nearby celestial objects but also plays a vital role in protecting the inner Solar System by deflecting or capturing comets and asteroids.
 
• Jupiter’s strong gravity has contributed to the formation and stability of its extensive system of moons, including the four largest Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mars**

 
 
• Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is often referred to as the "Red Planet" due to its reddish appearance caused by iron oxide on its surface.
 
• The surface gravity on Mars is significantly weaker than Earth, measured at approximately **3.71 m/s²**.
 
• Mars is much smaller and less dense than Jupiter, with a diameter of about 6,779 km.
 
• It is known for its thin atmosphere primarily composed of carbon dioxide and has the largest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons.
 
 
 
• **Neptune**
 
 
• Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun in the Solar System, classified as an ice giant due to its composition of water, methane, and ammonia ice.
 
• Its surface gravity is approximately **11.15 m/s²**, which is slightly stronger than Earth’s but much weaker than Jupiter’s.
 
• Neptune is famous for its deep blue color and has the strongest winds in the Solar System, reaching speeds of up to 2,100 km/h.
 
• It is smaller than Jupiter, with a diameter of approximately 49,244 km.
 
 
 
• **Uranus**
 
 
• Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and is classified as an ice giant, similar to Neptune.
 
• Its surface gravity is approximately **8.69 m/s²**, which is weaker than Earth’s and much weaker than Jupiter’s.
 
• Uranus is unique for its axial tilt, which causes it to rotate on its side, giving rise to extreme seasons.
 
• It has a diameter of about 50,724 km and a faint ring system.
 
 
 
• **Concept of Surface Gravity**
 
 
• Surface gravity refers to the gravitational acceleration experienced at the surface of a celestial body.
 
• The surface gravity of a planet depends on its mass and radius, with larger and denser planets exhibiting higher gravity.
 
• Gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn have lower densities but their immense mass results in stronger surface gravity compared to terrestrial planets.
